# Individual and Simultaneous Imaging of 99mTc and 177Lu with a Preclinical Broad Energy-Spectrum CZT-based SPECT

**Authors:** Pedro M. C. C. Encarnação; Pedro M. M. Correia; Baharak Mehrdel; Isabella Bredwell; João F. C. A. Veloso; Javier Caravaca; Youngho Seo

**Affiliations:** I3N - Physics Department, University of Aveiro, Portugal | Department of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging, University of California at San Francisco, San Francisco, CA 94143 USA. | Nuclear Science Division, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory 1 Cyclotron Rd. 94720 Berkeley CA USA and with the Department of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging, University of California at San Francisco, San Francisco, CA 94143 USA

## Abstract

Radiopharmaceutical therapy has demonstrated a high efficacy in the treatment of various tumor types. One of the radionuclides already used in the clinic is 177Lu, a beta emitter that also emits several photons imageable with SPECT. Quantitative imaging of 177Lu is critical for developing new radiopharmaceuticals. Energy resolution is an important factor when imaging multiple photon emissions. Solid-state detectors offer a superior performance over scintillators, that are commonly used in commercially-available preclinical SPECT scanners. This study demonstrates the feasibility of 99mTc and 177Lu quantitative imaging in mouse phantoms, individually and simultaneously, with a SPECT prototype built with four CdZnTe (CZT) detector heads and a custom-designed and energy-optimized parallel-hole tungsten collimator. With a custom implementation of the one-step late (OSL) image reconstruction algorithm, the system is capable of imaging energies from ~70 keV to 250 keV. Above 250 keV, images were significantly affected by septal penetration, consistent with the collimator design. A recovery coefficient within 25% was obtained for activities as low as 2 kBq/mL for 99mTc and 45% for 177Lu. Compared to a commercial NaI-based preclinical SPECT (VECTor4/CT), our prototype showed a superior energy resolution (< 5% at 140 keV), a similar uniformity with a high-compact design.

## Introduction

Preclinical imaging of radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) radionuclides is crucial to assess their biokinetics during their developmental phase [1]. The ability to perform quantitative imaging of the photon emissions of radionuclides using single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) opens up the possibility to monitor treatment and directly calculate delivered doses in tissue without the need of adjuvant agents or ex vivo techniques.

Quantitative SPECT (QSPECT) is particularly challenging for RPTs due to the intricate emission spectra of the radiopharmaceuticals used, which often present several gamma-ray emissions, some relatively close in energy. To quantify how RPT radiopharmaceuticals distribute within the patient, current solutions rely on novel hardware improvements, such as using high energy resolution semiconductors detectors [2], or on new advanced quantification techniques [3].

This field, commonly known as (radio)theranostics, has recently revived due to the clinical approval of 177Lu-based radiopharmaceutical therapeutics in the US (177Lu DOTATATE and 177Lu PSMA) by the Food and Drugs Administration, and in Europe (177Lu DOTATATE) by the European Medicines Agency for inoperable or metastatic pancreas or gastrointestinal tract cancers, known by their aggressiveness and low overall survival rate [4]. 177Lu is a therapeutic β − emitter with a moderately long half-life of 6.6 days.

An important aspect of 177Lu is that it also emits x-rays and six different γ rays, being 112.9 keV and 208.4 keV the ones with the highest intensity (Table I), facilitating direct imaging. Some of the emissions are relatively high energy, making imaging with SPECT cameras more challenging.

There is a large selection of preclinical SPECT systems commercially available (e.g., VECTor4CT by MILAbs [5], NanoSPECT or NanoScan by Mediso [6], Spark by Cubresa [7], γ -CUBE by MOLECUBES, Albira by BRUKER and γ -eye by BIOEMTECH). Currently, all of them are based on scintillator detectors. Despite their success, the energy resolution of scintillator detectors is limited compared to solid-state options like CdZnTe (CZT) and CdTe. Two CZT-based commercial options, which are no longer available, demonstrated superior energy resolution (eXplore speCZT by GE Healthcare [8] and X-SPECT by TriFoil [9]). RPT imaging relies on efficient detection of γ -ray emissions of various energies; thus factors like energy resolution, broad energy-range detection capability, and multi-emission imaging are gaining a special interest. CZT detectors have become popular in recent decades in nuclear imaging, especially for SPECT, due to their direct conversion of the photon energy into internal electric signal, enabling more compact geometry designs as well as due to their high stopping power and energy resolution compared to typical Sodium Iodide (NaI)-based detectors. In response to this, some research groups are exploiting the excellent energy resolution and stopping power of CZT or CdTe for preclinical SPECT for multi-isotope imaging (CdTe [10]) and imaging of alpha RPT (CZT [11], [12]). Other promising efforts include collimatorless detectors, such as Compton cameras [13], self-collimating cameras [14], or proximity cameras [15].

In our previous studies, we explored simulation of a custom-designed broad energy-spectrum multi-purpose tungsten collimator [16] and employed it in our CZT-based SPECT concept [17], [18]. We demonstrated quantitative imaging of 123I, 99mTc, and 177Lu without needing to change collimators in simulated clinical-size phantoms intended for brain and whole-body imaging applications such as metastatic cancer, radiotherapy treatment of gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors [19] or metastatic-castration-resistant prostate cancer [20].

In this paper, we report the first imaging results of a realization of a prototype of our SPECT detector intended for preclinical scenarios. A very important milestone in therapeutic radiopharmaceutical development is the assessment of in vivo biodistributions over time (i.e., biokinetics). For this reason, we focus our study on the quantification capabilities and the uniformity of mouse phantoms filled with 99mTc and 177Lu, individually and simultaneously. Finally, we compare the performance of our camera with a commercial preclinical SPECT system based on NaI(Tl) (VECTor4CT [5]).

## Methods

### Preclinical SPECT scanner

Our preclinical SPECT prototype consists of four rectangular heads (Fig. 1), each instrumented with CZT detectors and custom-designed parallel-hole tungsten collimators. The different parts are described in detail below.

#### Cadmium zinc telluride detectors:

Each detector head consists of five CZT modules (M1085 from Redlen Technologies, Saanichton, BC, Canada) of pixelated monocrystals of 25.6mm × 25.6mm with a pixel pitch of 1.6mm and a total of 16 × 16 pixels. The width of the streets (inactive space between pixels) are 0.2mm, leaving an active pixel area of 1.5mm × 1.5mm, except for the edge pixels which are 1.3mm wide. The CZT thickness is 5mm, and the detector is read out through a gold-plated cathode. The five modules are arranged in a 5 × 1 configuration, yielding a rectangular detector head of 128mm × 25.6mm. The detectors are enclosed in an stainless steel case embedded in a 3-mm thick lead case for shielding.

#### Front-end electronics and data acquisition system:

The final assembly of detectors was designed and built in collaboration with IDEAS (Oslo, Norway [23]) and based on their IDE-Gamma-Spect product. Each CZT module is operated by two ASICs, each controlling 128 pixels for a total of 256 pixels per module. This ASIC provides a dynamic range from ~50 keV to ~350 keV, and an energy resolution of 5% Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) at 122 keV reported by the manufacturer, and they can operate at rates of up to tens of kHz with an approximate deadtime of 1 μ s .

After ionizing radiation generates charge deposition in the CZT, the signal undergoes amplification and pulse shaping, and then converted to an ADC value. This is compared to a globally configurable threshold to determine whether the event will be recorded. For this analysis, the threshold is fixed to 9 digital channels, which approximately corresponds to 60 keV. We chose this threshold to avoid excessive noise triggers. Only the first pixel to trigger the acquisition is recorded. A controller is connected to the four detector heads to provide an interface between the system and the PC through the vendor’s application programming interface and graphical user interface.

Triggered data were buffered along with the pixel address (channel ID and ASIC ID), number of samples, timestamp, and other low level information. The data were initially stored in a CSV file generated by the IDEAS software and subsequently converted to a NumPy structured array to accelerate file loading during analysis time. This information was stored in list mode format accompanied by a header that includes the acquisition conditions (detector configuration, isotope, and exposure time). The final list mode data included corrections such as energy calibration or removal of multi-triggered events described in II-D2. Fig. 2 provides a schematic overview of the data flow from data scan to the final reconstructed image.

#### Parallel-hole tungsten collimators:

A custom-made tungsten collimator designed by our group [16] was manufactured by Nuclear Fields (Vortum-Mullem, The Netherlands [24]). The collimator design is optimized for photon energies up to ~250 keV. It features a pixel-matching geometry, with a pixel pitch of 1.6mm, a septal width of 0.32mm and a septal length of 23mm. The collimator is manufactured from tungsten foil to guarantee a very high density. The front face of the collimator is finished with a carbon sheet to protect the CZT detectors from ambient light. The back of the collimator is attached to a 3-mm thick lead base that fits on the lead shielding case hosting the CZT modules, forming a completely shielded box (Fig. 1).

#### System configuration:

The four detector heads are arranged around a box-shaped field-of-view (FOV) with dimensions 25.6mm × 25.6mm × 128mm. The heads are mounted on an aluminium structure, with a separation of 31.8mm and 33.6mm between two opposite heads (Fig. 1a), that allows precise alignment, with each head rotated 90° relative to the others, and their centers aligned with the FOV center (Fig. 1). Phantoms were deployed through the front bore without changing the detector configuration.

### Radionuclides

99mTc was purchased from a commercial radiopharmacy (Jubilant) and provided in the form of 99mTc pertechnetate. Three batches of 37MBq each were used for our experiment. The emission of a single 140.5 keV γ -ray with a 89% intensity is employed in our imaging analysis.

177Lu was sourced from the US Department of Energy Isotope program in its free form. Two batches of approximately 37MBq each were used.

### Phantoms

#### Mouse phantom:

A 3D-printed plastic mouse phantom (Fig. 3a) manufactured by BIOEMTECH (Athens, Greece [25]) is employed to characterize our system. It mimics approximately a 28 g mouse with fillable cavities designed in the shape of different organs and solid tumors (brain, thyroid, lungs, heart, liver, kidneys, bladder, top tumor and flank tumor). The cavities are not interconnected and can be filled independently with different solutions. The anatomical model is based on the Digimouse model, extracted from the anatomical and cryosection data [26], [27]. The approximate dimensions are 100mm × 30mm × 20mm and the total fillable volume is 4.2mL.

We use six mouse phantoms. One pair was filled with 2.1MBq/mL and 7.2MBq/mL of 99mTc. The second pair was filled with 8.5MBq/mL and 0.5MBq/mL of 177Lu, and the third pair was filled with cavities alternating between 5.3MBq/mL of 99mTc and 3.2MBq/mL of 177Lu. Activities at imaging time are quoted for each experiment in each relevant section. These activities are of the order of those injected to mice in typical 99mTc and 177Lu experiments (30–37 MBq or 1.2–1.5 MBq/g assuming the weight of an average adult mouse being 25 g) [28], [29].

#### Uniform phantom:

We employed a box-shaped phantom (Fig. 3 b)) with inner dimensions equivalent to the FOV (25.6mm × 25.6mm × 128mm) filled at a uniform concentration to assess the uniformity of the detector’s sensitivity. The phantom was custom-designed and 3D-printed using Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) and finished with an acetone vapor polishing treatment to make the surfaces waterproof and prevent leakage.

Two phantoms were filled with 0.6MBq/mL of 99mTc and with 2.6MBq/mL of 177Lu, respectively. Datasets were acquired over a 60-minute period, and the sensitivity response for the four detector heads was subsequently generated. The acquired response was used later in the image reconstruction process.

### System Calibration

#### Preprocessing:

To guarantee high-quality images several steps are undertaken to ensure the accuracy of detectors heads data acquired. Initially, data readout errors were identified and removed from the list mode which include corrupted data generated at the beginning of each dataset and multi-trigger events. The former correspond to approximately 20 events written at the start of a new acquisition and easily identified by the out-of-range pixel identifier. The latter were caused by multiple pixels triggering within the same detector response timing window, resulting in an erroneous pixel address since the system’s readout cannot properly handle multi-pixel events. They are also easily identified by a raised flag in the data packet. The number of rejected events due to these readout errors is very small and does not affect the quantification since we perform an in-situ calibration.

#### Energy Calibration:

Since the detector activity operational regime varies between 50 and 350 keV and 177Lu emits γ s between 71.6 keV and 321.3 keV, this radionuclide is well suited to perform the system’s energy calibration. The uniform phantom filled with 177Lu was used for this purpose.

Fig. 4 a) shows a 2D histogram with the CZT unique identifier (Detector pixel) versus the ADC channel triggered (ADC value). Each column displays an intensity map of the energy response for each CZT pixel in which it is possible to notice a different response for each CZT. For this reason, each detector needs to be calibrated individually.

For each column, a peak detection function developed by [30] was employed. To improve the peak detection and taking into consideration the peaks’ relative intensity, each 1D histogram was divided into two: one from 0 to 5500 ADC values and the other from 5500 to 8192. This technique made the peak identification more robust.

After the peaks were obtained, an order-two polynomial fit was performed on the data to obtain the correct coefficients for each pixel and store in a calibration file. For new acquisitions, each event calibrated energy was determined by the individually coefficients of the CZT pixel in which the event was detected.

#### Energy resolution and energy window:

To assess the energy resolution dependency with the energy of the γ s emitted, the energy resolution was determined for the 4 peaks of 177Lu with higher predominance and the 59.3 keV characteristic x-ray emission from the tungsten. Initially, the scatter contribution was estimated using a linear function. The slope of this function was calculated based on the ratio between two values: the difference in the number of counts at energies ±10 keV from the photo-peak position and the 20 keV difference in energy between these positions. Subsequently, this contribution was subtracted from the peaks, a Gaussian fitting was applied to each peak and the energy resolution determined by the FWHM and the peaks’ energies. As it is shown in Section III-A2, the system energy resolution, E r , peak , follows a behaviour determined by (1) E r , peak = p 1 E peak + p 2 where E peak is the expected photopeak energy, p 2 is a constant and p 1 is the Fano factor, which is determined by detector material and weakly dependent, with the exception at low energies, on the incident radiation energy [31].

Regarding the energy window selection, the upper ( E max ) and lower ( E min ) energy thresholds for each emission were based on the energy resolution ( E r , peak ) at each peaks measured in II-E. We used a lookup table with the decay information of radioisotope, defining the thresholds as function of E peak given by (2) E max , min = E peak × 1 ± E r , peak

#### Detector spatial and energy response:

The CZT pixels in each detector can have different responses due to different factors. The main ones are manufacturing or material variability and geometric factors due to the different active area of edge pixels.

To evaluate the relative response between the CZT pixels, the uniform phantom filled with 177Lu was used. The data was filtered for 177Lu at 112.9 and 208.4 keV emissions and the response was evaluated for each detector head. Fig. 4 c) illustrates a heat map depicting the spatial response of head 4, and the correspondent profile sums in the x and z directions. The response of each detector was used in the system response matrix (SRM) calculation to optimize image quality and accuracy.

#### Absolute Activity Calibration:

Output images were converted from raw counts to activity per volume (MBq/mL) by deploying known activity concentrations A c and retrieving the count rate C r within a certain energy window. A calibration factor Q f is calculated using the same mouse phantoms used for imaging as (3) Q f = A c C r V v where V v is the voxel volume. Calibrated images were obtained by multiplying raw images voxel by voxel by this calibration factor. These factors depend on isotope type and energy window and are calculated individually for each emission of 99mTc and 177Lu.

### Custom-made reconstruction framework

A dedicated image reconstruction framework was developed in Python™ [32], using CUDA programming (version 11.3 [33]) for accelerated computing with of NVIDIA Graphical processing units (GPUs). The framework enabled us the production of high-quality images in few seconds. The framework makes use of several scientific and numeric libraries, including PyCUDA [34] (version 2021.1), NumPy [35] (version 1.21), and Pandas (version 2.1.0) [36]. Matplotlib (version 3.7) [37] is employed for generating 2D graphs, while VTK (Visualization Toolkit, v.9.2) [38] with the Python API is utilized for 3D volume rendering. SciPy version 1.7 [39] was used to determine the energy calibration coefficients for each detector pixel as explained in Section II-D2. Additionally, it was used to fit a Gaussian function to the system’s energy resolution data for different energy peaks and to predict its behaviour at various energy levels according to Equation 1 in Section II-D3.

#### Geometric mapping:

To accurately determine the parametric position of the triggered detector regarding the image space, a lookup table containing the focal point and the vertices of the collimator correlated with ASICs and detector heads map was created for each detector head. For every event recorded in the raw list mode, a new list mode or sinogram was generated, incorporating the parametric information derived from the events and necessary to construct the projector.

#### Pyramidal Projector:

Fig. 5 showcases the pyramidal projector developed, constructed using four planes (only the surfaces and the (dashed) lines of intersection of those planes are shown). These planes were determined by the focal point (highlighted in red) and the frontal vertices of the collimator (depicted in blue). The position of the focal point was established at the intersection point of the lines created from the vertices of the CZT pixels (in gold), and the opposite vertices of the collimator (green dots).

#### GPU implementation:

A dedicated GPU One Step Late (OSL) algorithm was developed. The OSL is a Bayesian iterative reconstruction method, initial proposed by [40], to reduce the noise that amplifies with the number of iterations in iterative algorithms such as the Maximum Likelihood Expectation Method (MLEM) [41], [42]. The noise is reduced by applying a penalized term after each iteration. We used the Median Root prior (MRP) [43] as penalizing term, defining the iteration step as (4) γ M R P n e w = 1 1 + β γ ( i ) − M e d ( γ , i ) M e d ( γ , i ) γ = γ M R P old γ MLEM new ( i ) where γ MLEM n e w ( i ) is the pixel value at i iteration given by the MLEM algorithm, β is the Bayesian parameter setting the prior’s weight, Med corresponds to the median of image pixels over a kernel of a certain size. The kernel size and β values typically range between 3 to 5 and 0.05 to 0.3, respectively. In our case (kernel = 3 and β = 0.15 ), these values were chosen to reduce the noise in the image without affecting its resolution or causing structure loss.

Regarding the implementation design, the forward and back-projection are the algorithm segments which benefits the most from GPU acceleration. To take advantage of the GPU architecture and achieve an optimal performance without losing image quality, the forward projection uses an event-driven approach, eliminating potential race conditions [44], while the backprojection uses a voxel-driven approach, previously applied with resource of GPUs by [45]–[47] in Positron Emission Tomographic (PET) image reconstruction applications, and initial proven by [48]. A pseudo-code version of our algorithm segments implemented in the GPU can be found in the appendix A.

#### Quantitative Imaging:

The imaging performance of the system was characterized using mouse phantoms and for the different emissions of 99mTc and 177Lu. Cylindrical regions of interest (ROIs) were manually drawn for each organ and tumors using the software AMIDE [49]. The ROIs were chosen such that they were fully contained within the active region. The measured activity concentration was compared to the true activity concentration defining a recovery coefficient (RC) for each organ as: (5) C r v = C r V R O I × Q f ¯ (6) RC = C r v A c where the C r is the count rate (cps) in the ROI, V Roi is the ROI volume (in ml), the Q f is the quantification factor (Equation 3), and A c is the prepared activity concentration in the phantom.

RCs were calculated for decreasing concentrations for each emission. Lower concentrations were emulated by randomly eliminating counts from the datasets uniformly in time.

#### Algorithm convergence:

To determine the optimal number of iterations required for reconstructing images, the mouse phantom filled with 99mTc dataset was used. The images were reconstructed with the MRP algorithm for a β value of 0.15 and a kernel size of 3, iterating 30 times, and stored at intervals of two iterations. Subsequently, these images were divided by the acquisition time length and voxel volume and then multiplied by the quantification factor (Equation 5) established using liver data obtained at the 30 t h iteration. For each iteration, a spherical ROI with a 2 mm radius was designated at the liver, whose position was determined by calculating its center of mass with the support of a segmented BIOEMTECH mouse phantom. For each ROI, we compute the mean value and standard deviation, defined as (7) μ C r v = 1 N ∑ i = 1 N C r v ( i ) (8) σ C r v = 1 N ∑ i = 1 N C r v ( i ) − μ C r v 2 where C r v ( i ) represents the count rate per unit of volume at each pixel within the ROI, μ C r v is the mean count rate per unit of volume and N is the total number of pixels within the ROI. These were used to quantify the image uniformity through the coefficient of variation (CV) [50] given by Equation 9.

$$ (9) C V R O I = σ C r v μ C r v × 100 $$

### Sensitivity

The sensitivity S was calculated using the mouse phantom in order to compute it in a realistic scenario that included photon attenuation and a radionuclide distribution relevant for mice imaging. We exclusively used 99mTc to minimize septal penetration and interference from other emissions. It is defined as (10) S = N D T × A where N D is the total number of detected counts in the photopeak energy window, T is the exposure time, and A is the true activity in Bq. An alternative definition of the sensitivity S E takes into account the size of the energy window and it is defined as (11) S E = S E w where E w is the size of the photopeak energy window in keV.

### Comparison with commercial preclinical SPECT scanner

The VECTor4CT preclinical scanner (MILabs, The Netherlands [5]) was used to benchmark our system. This conventional preclinical SPECT/CT scanner is equipped with three 3/8-inch thick NaI detectors in a triangular shape and a multipinhole collimator. For this work, the high-energy ultrahigh-resolution, rat and mouse multi-pinhole collimator (M7 HE-UHR-RM) was used. From the vendor specifications, this 98mm-diameter collimator has several clustered pinholes [51] with 1.8 mm diameter apertures, and provides a spatial resolution of 1.5 mm and a 1.1% sensitivity for a small field of view. Imaging experiments were carried out using equivalent mouse phantoms under equivalent conditions of activity concentration and acquisition time that with our experimental camera. Image reconstruction was performed using the vendor’s software (POSEM [52]) with 128 subsets and 10 iterations and a post-processing Gaussian filter of 2.4 mm and a kernel of 15. The triple energy window scattering correction [53] was applied, along with the CT-based attenuation correction [54] for the quantitative comparison. Qualitative imaging experiments did not include the corrections in order to compare both systems under the same conditions.

## Results

### System Calibrations

#### Energy calibration:

The Fig. 4 b) depicts the CZT individual energy response to the uniform phantom filled with 177Lu after employing the method described in II-D2. The data showing an alignment of the CZT spectral response enhancing the system’s global energy resolution through this correction, allowing a more precise peak identification.

#### Energy resolution:

The 71.6 keV and 136.7 keV peak are not distinguishable in the spectrum due to a combination of low branching ratio and the background from scattering and tungsten characteristic x-rays. While the higher energy γ s are visible above the background noise, they are not as clear as the 112.9 keV and 208.4 keV peaks, in line with the intensity data in Table I.

The tungsten’s characteristic x-ray emissions are at 57.9, 59.3, 67.2, and 69.1 keV [55]. The collimator-induced x-ray peaks with higher intensity (59.3 and 67.7 keV) are also visible in the spectra of 177Lu and 99mTc, highlighted in grey in Fig. 4 e) and Fig. 12 in appendix.

The x-ray emissions from 177Lu, ranging from 7 to 65 keV remain undetected by our CZT system. This lack of detection can be attributed to limitations in the system electronics readout electronics and the x-ray contributions of the tungsten.

Fig. 4 d) illustrates the energy resolution across the γ emission energy spectrum, revealing an improvement in resolution with increasing energy, ranging from 8.6% for 59.3 keV to 1.8% for 321 keV. A fit using Equation 1 was employed, and used to set the energy window across the system operation range. A similar energy resolution behaviour using a CZT detector and a 177Lu was reported by [56], ranging from ~13% to ~3% in the same energy interval.

#### Detector spatial and energy response variation:

As shown in the heat maps of Fig. 4 c), the peripheral CZT pixels of each module exhibit a lower counts number (green stripes) due to their smaller area of detection, resulting in a drop in sensitivity leading to the creation of artifacts if not corrected.

Additionally, along the edges of the detector head in the x direction, a sensitivity decrease is noticeable. Besides the CZT area of detection, this effect is mainly caused by the source’s shape and dimensions (pink stripes), which matches the detector head design, leading to fewer emitted γ s reaching the CZT pixels at detector head edge. Since these data contribute to the computation of the SRM, the drop in sensitivity caused by the uniform source will create of high-intensity voxels, as the acquired data may not accurately reflect the true pixel sensitivity in these regions. To correct this effect, the probability of detection for these pixels was set as the mean response of the non-peripheral CZT detectors, which are placed at maximum distance of 9.6 mm and 60.8 of the centre’s head, regarding its width and length, respectively. The coronal and transverse view of SRM sum is show in 4 f). Furthermore, regarding the system’s energy response variation, as illustrated in Fig. 4 c), the heat maps and profiles for the 112.9 keV and 208.4 keV peaks exhibit similar responses, suggesting a consistent system response across different levels of energy.

### Algorithm convergence

Fig. 6 shows the algorithm convergence according with RC and uniformity values within the liver ROI. The RC reaches 0.95 after 11 iterations, varying 0.2% per iteration after the 20 t h , indicating convergence of the algorithm. However, beyond this point, the standard deviation continues to rise, signifying image degradation without enhancing RC values. As for uniformity, a value of 18.7% is reached after 20 iterations.

### Imaging performance

#### Sensitivity:

The sensitivity was measured with a mouse phantom filled with a known total activity of 99mTc. We obtain an S of 132 cps/MBq and an S E of 13.2 cps/MBq/keV.

#### Response across system operation range:

Fig. 7 shows the weighted average of the slices within a 20mm thickness centred at the phantom centre, taken at six peak locations of 177Lu. These images were reconstructed using 20 iterations, a voxel size of 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.8 mm3, employing the MRP algorithm with a β value of 0.15 and a kernel size of 3. Upon visual inspection, it is evident that the higher intensity γ emissions (112.9 keV and 208.4 keV) yield better-resolved images, with all organs clearly distinguishable. However, discerning the gap between the lungs may require adjustments to the color map. For γ -ray energies of 250 keV and 321 keV, image deterioration is noticeable, particularly worse for 321 keV. This degradation derives from two factors. First, the high energy of the γ rays allows them to penetrate the collimator walls, altering the angle of acceptance to CZT detectors. As the reconstruction model does not take into consideration this effect, image quality is affected. Second, the signal-to-noise ratio between the peak and background is significantly lower for these energies compared to 112.9 and 208.4 keV peaks, further contributing to image degradation.

#### Imaging response versus activity concentration:

Images acquired with our system of a mouse phantom filled with 99mTc are shown in Fig.8 a). These correspond to the weighted average of the coronal projections included in a 10mm thick region, after being filtered with a 3D median filter (kernel size 3). All the organs are clearly visible at high activity concentration. As expected, image quality decreases as the radionuclide concentration decreases. The RC for each organ as a function of the activity concentration is shown in Fig. 8 b). For high concentrations, the RC is close to the unity, with fluctuations up to 40%. The RC behaves similarly even at low concentrations of 1 kBq/mL. Fluctuations on the RC increase to up to 60–80% for lower concentrations. The relative uncertainty (or uniformity) is monitored across activity concentrations in Fig. 8 c), with a very similar behaviour to the RC.

Results for a similar experiment with 177Lu are in Fig.9 for the 112.9 keV and the 208 keV emissions, respectively. These are the γ -ray emissions with highest intensity. Image quality are very similar between them and compared to 99mTc. Except for the right lung, with a downward fluctuation of 50%, the RC for the rest of the organs are within 35% of the expected values. Image quality visually decreases at low concentration, but with RCs relatively unchanged up to the tested concentration of 261 Bq/mL. Relative uncertainties remain fairly constant at a value close to 10% up to concentrations of 5 kBq/mL, when they start increasing up to more than 40% for the lowest concentration of 261 Bq/mL.

### Comparison with commercial system

A similar analysis presented in the previous section was performed for both our system and a commercial preclinical SPECT featuring NaI and multi-pinhole collimation. Scatter and attenuation corrections were applied for the images of the commercial system, as recommended by the vendor. A 0.4mm Gaussian filter is applied to the final images followed by a median 3D filter with a kernel of 3. The uniformity obtained for 99mTc and the two main emissions of 177Lu (112.9 keV and 208.4 keV) are shown in Fig.10. This analysis indicates that our approach results in a higher uniformity than the commercial option for the three energies.

We further compared the performance of our system versus the commercial NaI option for simultaneous imaging of 99mTc and 177Lu. We imaged a mouse phantom whose organs were filled alternatively with each isotope. At the time of imaging, the activity concentrations were 0.33 MBq/mL for 99mTc and 2.9 MBq/mL for 177Lu. The energy spectra obtained with both systems are compared in Fig. 11 a), where the superior energy resolution of our system was demonstrated. Images were reconstructed with both systems and shown in Fig. 11 b). None of the images included scatter or attenuation correction in order to be compared under the same conditions. Both systems were able to retrieve images of 99mTc and the two main 177Lu emissions. Small image artifacts are observed for the 112.9 keV emission of 177Lu for both system, due to a leakeage of 99mTc photopeak counts into the 177Lu energy window. This is not observed for the 208.4 keV emission of 177Lu, which rules out a cross-contamination in the organ volumes.

## Discussion

We have shown that a CZT-based preclinical SPECT can obtain quantitative images of 99mTc and 177Lu biodistributions in mouse phantoms. Performance could be improved with more detector heads or adding rotation or swiveling [18]. We focused our study on the performance characterization of quantification of organ biodistributions in mice, rather than delivering a thorough characterization of our system. The current purpose is to evaluate a CZT camera for quantitative RPT imaging, in particular of 177Lu, and the standard imaging radionuclide such as 99mTc. We have demonstrated that our SPECT system, consisting of a multi-purpose broad energy-spectrum collimator and CZT, is able to perform quantitative imaging of 99mTc and 177Lu in mouse phantoms with RCs for individual organs close to unity within ~ 25% for 99mTc concentrations of 2.1 kBq/mL and within ~ 50% for 177Lu concentrations of 261 Bq/mL, respectively. Relative uncertainties are of the order of 10% for 99mTc concentrations higher than 2.1 kBq/mL and 177Lu concentrations higher than 5.2 kBq/mL. This informs of the precision of our system to obtain biodistributions of 99mTc or 177Lu.

The quantitative imaging precision and accuracy are comparable to that of a commercial NaI-based pre-clinical SPECT [5]. This means that our CZT systems can provide a more compact solution and more flexibile geometry with similar performance than NaI systems, which facilitates a benchtop system which can be shielded from external backgrounds. The maximum deviations of 35% on the calculated RC are comparable to other studies with clinical systems where deviations of more than 30% are measured [57]. This deviations are mostly attributed to partial volume effects and an heterogeneous response within the FOV [58].

Our simultaneous 99mTc and 177Lu imaging experiment shows a slightly better image quality than that of NaI systems. For a 177Lu to 99mTc concentration ratio of 9:1, the contamination of 99mTc counts into the 112.9 keV energy window of 177Lu is slightly higher than for the NaI system due to the characteristic low energy tailing effect of CZT [59]. No evidence of contamination in the 99mTc window due to the 208.4 keV 177Lu peak is observed. Thus, the recommendation is to use a high 177Lu:99mTc concentration ratio in order to minimize these effects.

An important advantage of our CZT system is its good energy resolution below 5% at 140.5 keV, better than NaI-based systems (~ 10%) and comparable to those obtained in previous CZT systems [8], [9]. The measured value is also lower than what we projected in our clinical simulation studies in [18] (6.5%). The system’s energy resolution improves with γ -ray energy, reaching 1.8% at 321.3 keV. This energy resolution could help to better resolve γ -ray emissions that are very close in energy. The superior energy resolution could be more relevant with other RPT radionuclides with a greater number of emissions, such as to clearly distinguish between the 225Ac emissions below 250keV, or for simultaneous imaging of very close emission lines like those of 99mTc and 123I [60]. Moreover, the energy resolution in CZT can be further improved by depth of interaction corrections in dual-readout systems with 3D positioning [61]–[63].

We obtained a sensitivity (132 cps/MBq) comparable to those measured in other commercialized CZT systems (180 cps/MBq for X-SPECT [9] and 139 cps/MBq to 313 cps/MBq for eXplore speCZT [8]), and the developmental system CdTe-DSD SPECT-I (121 cps/MBq [10]). The proposed Alpha-SPECT, also featuring CZT, intends to reach 2000 cps/MBq for a larger FOV than our system with a new collimator concept, but its performance has been only demonstrated in simulation [11], [12]. Our sensitivity is lower than that of VECTor4CT for an equivalent FOV (603 cps/MBq) due to their large number of pinholes. In spite of the lower sensitivity, our image quantification studies reveal a very similar response for both systems in the considered scenario. Although pinhole scanners are more common in small-animal SPECT, we choose parallel-hole collimation to leverage our design intended for clinical purposes. This type of collimator generally requires less detector surface, since it is not magnifying, which is advantageous to have a more compact design that can be better shielded, and to reduce collimator and CZT detector costs. Another advantage of our collimators is that they use substantially less material than standard multi-pinhole collimators, which reduces the scattering component in the collimator. A disadvantage with respect to pinhole collimation is that the spatial resolution is still limited by the parallel hole collimator itself without any magnification possibility. And, our current detector and collimator designs do not allow energies above 250 keV to be imageable quantitatively. In addition, a faded checker pattern is observed in Figs. 8 a) and 9 b) that correspond to an artifact generated by the pitch of the pixel and the septa. This effect might impact the quantification for ROIs smaller than the pixel pitch, which is not the case in this analysis. Oblique detector views or dedicated corrections would likely make this pattern disappear.

Regarding the energy range in our imaging system, 177Lu images obtained with the 208.4 keV present similar quality than those with 112.9 keV emissions. We can obtain images distinctly identifiable above background noise up to the 321.3 keV emission. However, images above 249.7 keV start quickly degrading due to septal penetration. This is a downside of our parallel-hole collimator, as opposed to collimators designed for high energy over 250 keV. Other dedicated parallel-hole collimators could be designed for higher energies to mitigate this issue. As for the x-ray emissions from 177Lu, they remain undetected due to overlap with the characteristic x-ray emission of tungsten in the ~53 keV to ~74 keV region.

## Conclusions

We have demonstrated that our CZT-based SPECT system with custom tungsten collimators provides a high energy-resolution and compact system for quantitative imaging of 99mTc and 177Lu in mice. Its performance between 70 keV and 250 keV is similar to commercial NaI-, pinhole-based options in terms of quantification and uniformity up to the levels of spatial resolution required for organ biodistributions. We demonstrate simultaneous imaging of 99mTc and 177Lu with a ratio 1 to 10. Low 99mTc concentrations are recommended to mitigate image artifacts in co-imaging experiments. Future improvements include implementation of corrections due to scatter in the subject and the collimator, attenuation correction for better quantification, and enabling imaging of γ -rays with energies above 250 keV with a dedicated exchangeable high-energy collimator as needed. The excellent energy resolution of our system will likely have a larger impact for other therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals with several emissions below 250 keV, such as 225Ac, or for co-injection experiments with γ -ray emitters whose emissions are very close in energy (e.g., 123I and 99mTc).
